reason: The passage demonstrates this principle through David's response to his sin of numbering Israel. When David realizes his error has brought divine judgment and a plague upon the people, he explicitly takes full responsibility, stating 'I am the one who sinned and done wrong' (וַאֲנִי־ הוּא אֲשֶׁר־ חָטָאתִי). Critically, he acknowledges that the people themselves bear no blame: 'These sheep, what have they done?' (וְאֵלֶּה הַצֹּאן מֶה עָשׂוּ). David then demonstrates accountability and concern for the people's welfare by pleading with God: 'May your hand be upon me and my house, not upon your people' (תְּהִי נָא יָֽדְךָ בִּי וּבְבֵית אָבִי וּֽבְעַמְּךָ לֹא לְמַגֵּפָה), actively interposing himself between the people and punishment. Finally, he takes concrete remedial action by building an altar and offering sacrifices. The passage illustrates that good leadership requires leaders to accept accountability for their decisions and prioritize their people's welfare over their own interests.
